name: heard.dev
tagline: A hosted place to collect user feedback and feature requests for a software product.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Feedback collection is one of the most cloneable categories in SaaS: a form, a list, votes, statuses, and an email when something ships. An agent can produce a working public board plus an admin view in a single session, and the data model fits on one page of schema. The hard parts are not technical, they are editorial: triaging, replying, and actually closing the loop, and no tool fixes that. Public detail on this particular product is thin, so treat the verdict as a judgment on the category rather than on any specific feature list. If it turns out to bundle deep issue tracker sync or in-app widgets across platforms, nudge this toward kinda.
coreLoopDIY: A public feedback board where users submit and upvote requests, and an admin marks them planned, shipped, or declined.
requirements: A machine or small VPS to host it
SMTP credentials if you want status-change emails
A domain or subdomain if the board should be public
whatYouLose: A polished embeddable widget that drops into your own app in one line
Spam and duplicate handling that works without you babysitting it
Integrations that push accepted requests into Linear, Jira, or GitHub
Changelog and announcement features that usually ship alongside the board
Someone else owning uptime for a page your users see
moatNotes: The defensible part of feedback tools is the widget, the dedupe, and the handoff into whatever issue tracker you already use. The board itself is a weekend.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a feedback board is the kind of thing you build once, deploy, and then quietly stop maintaining while your users keep posting into it. Paid tools keep the embed working across your marketing site and your app, handle the spam, dedupe near-identical requests, and give you a changelog to point at when you finally ship something. For a solo project the self-hosted version is genuinely fine. For anything with real volume, the money buys you not having to think about a page that is public and permanently judged.
notes: Public details on this one are thin, so the entry judges the category, not the marketing copy.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted user feedback and feature request board. One app, runs locally or on a small VPS.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js with the App Router and TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/feedback.db
- Drizzle ORM for schema and migrations
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- Nodemailer for optional email, SMTP config from .env

Data model:
- posts: id, title, body, author_email (nullable), status (open, planned, in_progress, shipped, declined), board, created_at
- votes: id, post_id, voter_key, created_at, unique on (post_id, voter_key)
- comments: id, post_id, body, is_admin, created_at
- boards: slug, name, description

Public side:
- /b/[board] lists posts, sortable by votes or newest, filterable by status
- Anyone can submit a post with title, body, and optional email
- Upvote with one click, identity is a signed cookie voter_key, no login
- /p/[id] shows the post, its comments, and a status badge
- Simple honeypot field plus a per-IP rate limit in middleware, no captcha service

Admin side:
- /admin behind a single password from ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env, session in an httpOnly cookie
- Change status, pin, merge one post into another (votes and comments move over, old post redirects)
- Reply as admin on any post
- When status changes, email everyone who submitted or commented with an email, only if SMTP vars are set, otherwise log to console

Also ship:
- GET /api/boards/[slug]/posts returning JSON so you can render the board elsewhere
- A seed script with two boards and about fifteen plausible posts
- README with setup, .env.example, and one command to run

Out of scope: OAuth, multi-tenancy, billing, embeddable widget, changelog pages, analytics, telemetry of any kind. Do not add an external service for anything. Keep it under roughly 1200 lines and make npm run dev work on the first try.
